client: I've been really struggling since last week when my team missed a major deadline at work. I just started this project manager role a few months ago, and I feel like everything is falling apart — like I'm constantly drowning in tasks and expectations I can't keep up with. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — stepping into a new leadership role is already a big adjustment, and missing that deadline probably made everything feel even more precarious and overwhelming. I'm really glad you decided to give this a shot, even with that doubt in the back of your mind, because that kind of honesty is actually a great starting point for us to work together. When you say everything feels like it's falling apart, what's the thought that tends to hit you hardest in those moments?

client: Honestly, the thought that hits hardest is something like "you're not actually qualified for this, and everyone's about to find out." It just loops in my head, especially when I make a mistake like that deadline thing — it feels like proof that I don't belong in this role. And then I start wondering if my team is already losing confidence in me, even if they haven't said anything.
therapist: That thought — "everyone's about to find out I don't belong here" — is such a painful one to carry, and it makes sense that a setback like the deadline would feel like it confirms it, even if the fuller picture might tell a different story. What you're describing sounds a lot like impostor syndrome, where our mind selectively grabs onto mistakes as "proof" while quietly ignoring all the evidence that led someone to trust you with this role in the first place. I'm curious — if you were to look at the other side of the evidence, what might someone who *does* believe in your abilities point to?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically that there must be some reason they hired me, but when I try to think of examples right now, my mind just goes kind of blank. Like, I know I've had good feedback before, but in this moment it all feels distant and almost irrelevant, like it doesn't count the same way the mistake does. I guess I'm also a little skeptical that just listing out the positives is really going to change how real this fear feels in my gut.
therapist: That blank feeling when you try to access the positives is really common, and your skepticism is completely valid — just listing good things rarely melts away a fear that lives so deeply. What you're describing, where the mistake feels vivid and real while the successes feel distant and irrelevant, is actually a well-known pattern called the negativity bias, and it's worth exploring *why* your mind weights them so differently rather than just trying to stack up the positives. What do you think it would mean about you if the good feedback *did* count just as much as the mistake — does part of you resist that somehow?

client: I mean... if the good feedback counted just as much, I guess it would feel like I was letting myself off the hook too easily. Like, part of me thinks that if I stop holding onto that mistake so tightly, I'll just get careless and mess up again, maybe even worse. So yeah, maybe I do resist it, but it doesn't feel like a choice exactly — it feels more like a warning system I can't turn off.
therapist: What you just named is really insightful — that self-criticism doesn't feel like cruelty, it feels like *protection*, like it's the thing keeping you from slipping up again. But it's worth gently questioning that assumption: has holding onto mistakes this tightly actually made you perform better, or has it mostly just made you feel worse while the anxiety stays the same? I'm wondering, when you imagine a version of yourself that took the good feedback seriously *and* stayed accountable — does that feel impossible, or just unfamiliar?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way... I have to admit that holding onto the mistakes hasn't actually made me do better at work, it's just made me dread going in every morning. But when I try to imagine that version of myself you're describing, it doesn't feel impossible exactly, it feels almost suspicious, like if I stopped being so hard on myself I'd be letting my guard down and something would go wrong. It's like the self-criticism is the only thing I trust to keep me in line, even though I can see it's kind of exhausting me.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just said — you can see clearly that the self-criticism is exhausting you and not actually improving your work, and yet letting it go feels dangerous, like losing the only safety net you trust. That tension makes a lot of sense, but it also points to something worth exploring: the belief that you *need* harshness to stay accountable is itself just a thought, not a proven fact — and it might be one we can gently test over time. What do you think a more trustworthy inner voice might sound like, if it kept you accountable without the dread?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but honestly I'm not sure I even know what a kind inner voice would sound like — it feels almost foreign to me. Like, if I'm not pushing myself hard or telling myself I'm falling short, what's actually going to stop me from just... slacking off completely? I guess I'm scared that without the dread, there's nothing left to keep me moving.
therapist: It's really touching that you're sitting with this so honestly, even when it feels unfamiliar and a little scary — the fact that a kind inner voice feels *foreign* tells us something important about how long you've relied on this harsh one, not that kindness isn't possible for you. Here's a gentle reframe worth considering: motivation driven by dread tends to keep us just barely avoiding failure, while motivation driven by something we actually care about tends to be more sustainable and more *ours*. I'm curious — underneath all the fear of falling short, what is it that you actually *want* for yourself in this role, if the dread weren't part of the equation?

client: That's... a harder question than it sounds, honestly. When I try to imagine what I actually want, separate from the fear, it's like there's just this blank space where an answer should be. I think somewhere in there I want to feel like I'm genuinely good at what I do, like I actually belong in the role and people aren't just tolerating me — but saying that out loud feels almost embarrassing, like wanting too much.
therapist: What you just shared doesn't sound like wanting too much — it sounds like a very human need to feel competent and genuinely connected to the people you work with, and the fact that it feels embarrassing to want that is worth noticing in itself. That quiet longing — to truly belong, not just be tolerated — might actually be a much more honest and sustainable compass than the dread has ever been. I'm wondering, where do you think the idea came from that wanting to feel good at something is something you should be ashamed of?

client: I don't know, maybe it goes back to my parents always kind of downplaying achievements, like if you got excited about something you did well, it was seen as showing off or being arrogant. So I learned pretty early that wanting recognition or feeling proud was something to keep quiet about, almost like it was selfish. It's weird hearing you say it's "human" because part of me still braces for the judgment, like even talking about it now feels a little dangerous somehow.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — you didn't arrive at this harshness by accident, you were taught very early that pride and self-recognition were dangerous, and so you've been protecting yourself from judgment ever since, including right now in this conversation. That "dangerous" feeling you notice even here makes complete sense given that history, and it takes real courage to keep talking anyway. I want to gently ask — knowing now that this belief was something you *learned* rather than something that's simply true, does that shift anything, even slightly, in how you see it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with you, like intellectually I can follow the logic that it was something I was taught. But there's this other part that immediately pushes back and says, "okay, but what if they were right to teach you that, what if you really aren't someone who deserves to feel proud?" It's like knowing the origin of the belief doesn't automatically make it feel less true, you know?
therapist: You're touching on something really important — knowing *where* a belief comes from and truly *feeling* like it's no longer true are two very different things, and it's completely normal for the emotional truth to lag behind the intellectual one. But I want to gently turn that pushback question around: notice that your mind is asking "what if you don't deserve to feel proud" — but that's not actually evidence, it's just the old voice doing what it's always done to keep you small and safe. What would you say if a close friend came to you and said those exact words about themselves — "I'm not sure I deserve to feel proud of anything I do"?

client: I'd probably tell them that's ridiculous, that of course they deserve to feel proud of themselves. But it's easier to see it clearly when it's someone else, you know? When it's me, it just feels different, like the rules don't apply the same way.
therapist: That gap you just noticed — where compassion flows so naturally toward a friend but gets blocked when it turns toward yourself — is actually one of the most important things we've uncovered today, and you named it so clearly. The rules *do* apply to you the same way, but somewhere along the line you learned to exempt yourself from the kindness you'd freely give others, and that exemption has a cost. I'm wondering — what do you think it would take, even in small moments, to start treating yourself as someone who deserves the same basic compassion you'd offer a friend?
